summary: Specifies an FTP application layer gateway for IPv6-to-IPv4 translation. FTP is still widely used, and clients with only IPv6 need to reach IPv4-only FTP servers through translators, which requires handling addresses carried in FTP commands.

eli5.summary: Old-style file transfer sends addresses inside its messages, which confuses translators between the new and old internet. This describes a helper that fixes those messages as they go through.

questions: how does ftp work through ipv6 to ipv4 translation
what is the algs command in ftp
subtitle: A gateway that rewrites FTP commands so IPv6-only clients can fetch files from IPv4-only servers.

tldr.problem: FTP carries IP addresses inside its commands, so an IPv6-to-IPv4 translator cannot fix them up by looking at packet headers alone. Only extended passive mode works unchanged, yet many servers do not support it and some clients do not ask for it.
tldr.mechanism: An application layer gateway sits on the FTP control channel (port 21), turns EPSV into PASV and, where supported, EPRT into PORT, and rewrites the server's replies so the IPv6 client sees a valid answer.
tldr.outcome: Unmodified IPv6 FTP clients can do simple transfers with unmodified IPv4 servers. The RFC says updating clients and servers is the better fix, so the ALG is a fallback and should not be a set-and-forget deployment.

today: RFC 6384 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the text itself presents the ALG as a fallback, with updating clients and servers as the preferred fix.

sections.title: The FTP Address Problem
sections.content:
The original FTP (RFC 959) has active mode, where the server connects back to the client, and passive mode, where the server opens a port for the client. The PORT command has an IPv4 address as its argument, and the server answers PASV with an IPv4 address, so both are incompatible with IPv6. RFC 2428 fixed this with EPSV, where the server returns only a port number, and EPRT, where the client supplies an IPv4 or IPv6 address and a port.

Through an IPv6-to-IPv4 translator, only extended passive mode works unchanged. But a survey in April 2009 of 25 FTP sites found only 12 supporting EPSV over IPv4, and all 25 completed a transfer in traditional PASV mode. Further tests suggested about 65% of servers support EPSV successfully and around 96% support PASV. The command line client included with Windows supports only active mode.

Since operators deploying translation rarely control clients or servers, this RFC standardizes an FTP ALG for simple transfers between one client and one server. It applies to both stateless translation (RFC 6145) and stateful translation (RFC 6146).
sections.eli5: Old file-transfer messages have the street address written inside the letter, not just on the envelope. A translator only fixes the envelope, so someone has to fix the letter too.

sections.title: What the ALG Is For, and When to Use It
sections.content:
The RFC says the most robust fix is to update clients and servers, and recommends doing so where possible. The ALG exists for operators who have no influence over them, and is standardized so that different ALGs behave consistently and do less harm.

Operators are encouraged to deploy an FTP ALG only when clearly needed. Because the ALG turns EPSV commands that a server could have handled directly into PASV, it adds complexity and reduces robustness, so a "set and forget" policy is not recommended.

An ALG used with a stateful translator MUST support EPSV translation and MAY support EPRT translation. With a stateless translator it MUST support EPSV and SHOULD also support EPRT. EPRT support assumes the ALG and translator are in a single device.
sections.eli5: The best fix is to teach everyone the new way to talk. The helper is only for places where nobody can change the old machines.

sections.title: Control Channel Translation
sections.content:
The ALG intercepts all TCP sessions to port 21 for IPv6 destinations that map to IPv4 servers behind the translator. It speaks enough Telnet to read and re-issue commands and responses, and MUST refuse Telnet options other than those allowed by RFC 1123 without relaying them.

It can either terminate the IPv6 TCP session and open a new IPv4 session to the server, or translate control packets one by one. The second approach MUST track and update TCP sequence numbers and be able to split packets, because rewriting changes payload length. The ALG MUST also either preserve the semantics of the TCP urgent pointer or clear the URG bit.

If the client issues AUTH to negotiate security such as TLS, the ALG MUST stop translating and copy data transparently in both directions, so the client's commands become hidden from it. It SHOULD ignore the AUTH command if the server answers in the 4xx or 5xx range. For language negotiation (RFC 2640) the ALG MAY monitor it, ignore it, or block it by turning LANG into a NOOP and the reply into a 502.
sections.eli5: The helper sits in the middle of the phone call and repeats each sentence in the other side's dialect. If the two sides start speaking in secret code, it steps aside.

sections.title: Translating EPSV, EPRT and Port 20
sections.content:
EPSV to PASV. An ALG SHOULD translate every EPSV from the client into PASV and reformat the server's 227 reply as a 229 reply, unless it positively knows EPSV will work. It SHOULD ignore the IPv4 address in the 227 reply. If the client sends EPSV with an argument other than 2 the ALG MUST answer 522, and for EPSV ALL it MUST answer 504 instead of passing the command on.

EPRT to PORT. The ALG MAY translate EPRT to PORT when the address is the client's own control-channel IPv6 address. With a stateless translator it maps to the matching IPv4 address and MUST preserve the port number. With a stateful one it selects an unused port, creates a mapping first, and only then sends PORT to the server; once the TCP handshake completes the mapping SHOULD be narrowed to that session. Any other address SHOULD be passed along unchanged.

Default port 20. If the client uses neither passive nor port commands, the server connects from port 20. A stateless translator needs no extra work, and a stateful one MAY accept such connections that match an existing control session.

If a client issues both PASV and PORT, behavior is undefined, and implementations SHOULD simply translate commands as they occur. Any command the ALG does not translate MUST be passed to the server unmodified.
sections.eli5: The helper rewrites the meeting-place instructions so the other side can find the right door. Anything it does not understand is passed along exactly as written.

sections.title: The ALGS Command
sections.content:
ALGs MUST support a new command, ALGS, that lets a client query and set the ALG status. Real FTP servers MUST NOT act on it but MUST still reply, ideally with 202 or any 50x response used for unknown commands.

The three arguments are STATUS64, ENABLE64 and DISABLE64. After any of them the ALG MUST return a 216 response naming the translation in effect: NONE, EPSV or EPSVEPRT. If the ALG cannot set the requested mode, it still returns 216 with the current status. A missing or unknown argument SHOULD give a 504 or 502 error. Clients can use this to put the ALG into transparent mode for more complex behavior such as server-to-server transfers.
sections.eli5: A client can ask the helper whether it is switched on, or tell it to stop helping when it wants to do something fancy.

sections.title: Timeouts and NOOP Replacement
sections.content:
Control channels SHOULD NOT time out while a data channel is active, and a timeout of at least 30 seconds is RECOMMENDED for data channel mappings waiting for initial packets.

When a client command is not passed to the server, the ALG issues a NOOP instead to keep keepalive state synchronized, and the NOOP response MUST NOT be relayed to the client. The ALG MAY wait for the server's 200 reply and turn it into the response the client needs, so it only modifies server packets. If the server answers anything other than 200, the ALG SHOULD tear down the control session and log an error.
sections.eli5: If the helper decides not to pass a message on, it sends a harmless nudge so the server does not fall asleep and hang up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
FTP is mostly used without extra security, so an eavesdropper can read login credentials and an attacker who can modify packets can change the data. FTP can be used with TLS (RFC 4217) to solve this. The translation and the ALG do not change either situation.

However, when TLS or another authentication mechanism the ALG knows about is used, the ALG function is not performed, so only passive transfers from a server that implements EPSV or a client that supports PASV will succeed. For general FTP security considerations the RFC points to RFC 2577.
sections.eli5: The helper does not make file transfer safer or less safe. If the two sides lock their messages, the helper cannot read them, so it cannot help.
